evidence.field: PDF p.1282; printed p.1267; 六 entry
evidence.text: The 六 entry identifies the graph as a pictograph resembling a simple shelter. It says Shang oracle-bone forms resemble a shelter set on the ground and later forms emphasize the shelter wall; Qin small-seal form curves the two upper strokes inward, and clerical transformation changes them into a dot and horizontal stroke. It proposes a grass hut as the original meaning and 六 as an early graph for 廬, later borrowed for the numeral because the sounds were close. It also connects 六 with the yin line in the Changes. I directly inspected the full page image, including the 六 heading, glyph sequence, source notes, and complete paragraph; this is one attributed proposal, not conclusive evidence of the graph’s origin.
evidence.title: 字源, 2012 edition (catalogue search for ISBN 9787552800692)

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Multi-function Chinese Character Database)
evidence.field: 漢字甲骨部件分析：六; web page lines 122–127
evidence.text: The entry reports three explanations: early 六 and 入 may have been the same graph before strokes differentiated the numeral; 六 may depict a shelter and be an earlier graph for 廬 (attributed to 劉興隆); or 六 may be an early conventional counting mark. It regards the 易-based Shuowen explanation as unlikely to preserve the original meaning. It cites oracle-bone examples for cardinal use in 合集 32320 (“燎六羊”) and ordinal use in 合集 7775 (“今六月王入于商”), with later numeral examples in bronze and Warring States texts. Those usages support 六 as a numeral in the cited records but do not decide among the graphic-origin proposals.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析：六

evidence.source: 香港教育城相關字源資源
evidence.field: 字形解說; 六 entry lines 11–14
evidence.text: This page labels oracle-bone, bronze, small-seal, and standard forms and proposes that 六 resembles a frontal view of a shelter, was the earlier graph for 廬, and was later borrowed for the number. The source provides no independent evidence here for the shelter’s name or its pronunciation, so its sound-based borrowing explanation remains a proposal.
evidence.title: 字源考釋 - 六

evidence.source: Baxter, William H., and Laurent Sagart
evidence.field: Old Chinese reconstruction table, v1.1 (2014); entries 六 and 廬; system notes
evidence.text: The inspected table lists 六 ‘six’ as Mandarin liù, Middle Chinese ljuwk, Old Chinese *k.ruk, and 廬 ‘hut; inn; to lodge’ as Mandarin lú, Middle Chinese ljo, Old Chinese *[r]a. The authors explain that brackets mark uncertainty and their Middle Chinese forms are transcriptions based on historical sources, not reconstructions. The listed Old Chinese forms do not substantiate a sound match for the proposed 六←廬 borrowing; the table also cannot identify the name of an allegedly depicted shelter.
evidence.kind: primary reconstruction table and system description
evidence.title: Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1 (13 September 2014)

evidence.source: 中央研究院數位文化中心 / 漢字「六」：基本資料
evidence.field: Basic data; Unicode and reading/sense entries
evidence.text: The Academia Sinica character record identifies 六 as U+516D, lists readings including liu4 and lu4, and defines its first sense as the numeral sum of five and one. This supports a current dictionary meaning and recorded readings, not an ancient sound relationship or origin account.
evidence.title: 漢字「六」：基本資料

gaps: The 六 entry in 李學勤主編《字源》 was directly inspected on the supplied continuation scan: PDF page 1282, printed page 1267. The previous supplied scan is PDF page 1281, printed page 1266; it contains the 六 department heading and pronunciation lead but not the substantive 六 explanation. The corpus metadata lacks extracted printed-page numbers, but the printed numbers 1266 and 1267 are legible in the scans.

The graphic origin remains unsettled among differentiation from 入, a shelter/廬 proposal, and a conventional counting-mark proposal. The oracle-bone numeral examples cited by CUHK attest numeral use, not which origin account is correct.

The proposed hut-name borrowing is not independently established. The identity and pronunciation of the alleged depicted object are unrecovered in inspected evidence; Baxter–Sagart’s listed reconstructions for 六 and 廬 do not substantiate the suggested sound match.

CUHK cites cardinal and ordinal oracle-bone records, but I did not inspect the original inscription images or establish the precise dates of those individual records. Their relative chronology remains unresolved.

The original page 1282 scan was directly inspected from the local book repository; the supplied attachment itself contains page 1281 only. The image inspection is therefore of the repository scan, not of a supplied page-1282 attachment.

The required official Unicode per-character record for 六 returned an internal error. Local current-reading metadata exists, and an Academia Sinica record was opened, but neither is the mandated official Unihan click-through evidence.
